column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which type of cell does NOT have a nucleus?
column14: Eukaryotic cell
column15: Prokaryotic cell
column16: Plant cell
column17: Animal cell
column28: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus. Eukaryotic cells, including plant and animal cells, keep their DNA inside a nucleus.
column29: Plant cells and animal cells are the same main type of cell. Of the two cell-type names that are left, which one is the simpler, smaller cell?

column9: Memory trick from class: "pro means no." A prokaryote has no ___ to hold its DNA.
column20: nucleus|a nucleus|the nucleus|nuclei|neucleus|nucleous|nuclear membrane|a nuclear membrane|nuclear envelope|the nuclear membrane|a nuclear envelope|the nuclear envelope
column28: "Pro means no": a prokaryote has no nucleus, so its DNA is not wrapped in a membrane. A eukaryote keeps its DNA inside a nucleus, the cell's control center.
column29: Think of the control center of a eukaryotic cell.

column9: Which of these is a prokaryote?
column14: A yeast cell
column15: An onion skin cell
column16: An amoeba
column17: A bacterium
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Yeast (a fungus), an amoeba (a protist), and onion cells (a plant) all have a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes.
column29: In class, the example given for prokaryotes was one group of living things.

column9: Prokaryotic cells have many membrane-bound organelles.
column28: False. Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound organelles at all. Only eukaryotic cells have organelles wrapped in their own membranes.
column29: Which cell type has "numerous membrane-bound organelles" in the notes?

column9: Which of these is a membrane-bound organelle found only in eukaryotic cells?
column14: Ribosome
column15: Cell membrane
column16: Mitochondrion
column17: Cytoplasm
column28: Mitochondria are wrapped in membranes and are found only in eukaryotes. Ribosomes, the cell membrane, and cytoplasm are not membrane-bound organelles.
column29: Which choice is a structure inside the cell that has its own membrane wrapped around it?

column9: Which structure is found in BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
column14: Nucleus
column15: Mitochondria
column16: Golgi apparatus
column17: Ribosomes
column28: Every cell has ribosomes because every cell has to make proteins. The nucleus, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound structures found only in eukaryotes.
column29: Every cell needs to make proteins. Which structure does that job?

column9: Which organism is made of eukaryotic cells?
column14: E. coli
column15: Streptococcus (strep throat bacteria)
column16: A mushroom
column17: Salmonella
column28: A mushroom is a fungus, and fungi are eukaryotes. E. coli, Streptococcus, and Salmonella are all bacteria, which are prokaryotes.
column29: Three of these are bacteria. Which one is not?

column9: A cell that has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles is called a(n) ___ cell.
column28: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles. Animals, plants, fungi, and protists are made of eukaryotic cells.
column29: It is the opposite of a prokaryotic cell.

column9: According to the class notes, prokaryotes are always ___.
column14: unicellular (made of one cell)
column15: multicellular (made of many cells)
column16: acellular (not made of cells at all)
column17: made of cells that contain a nucleus
column28: Prokaryotes are always unicellular: each bacterium is one complete cell. They are made of a cell (unlike viruses, which are not cells), and that cell has no nucleus.
column29: Think about a single bacterium. How many cells is it?

column9: Which statement about cell size is usually true?
column14: Prokaryotic cells are larger than eukaryotic cells.
column15: Eukaryotic cells are larger than prokaryotic cells.
column16: Both types of cells are always the same size.
column17: Prokaryotic cells are too large to see with a microscope.
column28: A typical bacterium is about 2 µm long, while eukaryotic cells such as cheek cells are about 60 µm. Eukaryotes are usually much larger and more complex.
column29: A bacterium is about 2 µm. A cheek cell is about 60 µm.

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Prokaryote :: A cell with no nucleus
column15: Eukaryote :: A cell with a nucleus
column16: Organelle :: A "little organ": a specialized structure in a cell
column17: Unicellular :: Made of one cell
column28: Prokaryote = no nucleus. Eukaryote = nucleus. Organelle = "little organ," a specialized structure. Unicellular = one cell. Multicellular = many cells.
column29: Look at the word parts in each term (uni-, multi-, pro-, eu-) and start with the pair you are surest of.

column9: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have a cell membrane.
column28: True. Every cell needs a boundary that controls what enters and leaves, so prokaryotes and eukaryotes both have a cell membrane.
column29: Could any cell survive without a boundary that controls what goes in and out?

column9: What shape is the DNA in a prokaryotic cell?
column14: A single circular loop
column15: Several straight (linear) chromosomes
column16: One long, straight (linear) strand
column17: Pairs of X-shaped chromosomes
column28: Prokaryotic DNA is a single circular loop with no ends. Straight (linear) chromosomes, including the X-shaped ones you see in pictures of dividing cells, belong to eukaryotes.
column29: Picture the DNA in the bacterium diagram from the notes. Which word fits it: circular (a closed loop) or linear (a straight line with two ends)?

column9: A biology club described six organisms without naming them. Which ones are eukaryotes? Select all that apply.
column14: One cell whose DNA is wrapped in a membrane of its own
column15: One cell whose DNA floats loose in the cytoplasm
column16: Millions of cells working together as tissues
column17: One cell with no membrane-bound organelles at all
column18: One cell that uses mitochondria to release energy
column19: One cell that packages proteins in a Golgi apparatus
column28: DNA wrapped in a membrane of its own is a nucleus, so that cell is a eukaryote. Millions of cells working as tissues means multicellular, and prokaryotes are always one cell. Mitochondria and a Golgi apparatus are membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotes have. DNA floating loose in the cytoplasm means there is no nucleus, and a cell with no membrane-bound organelles at all is a prokaryote.
column29: Prokaryotes are always one cell and have no membrane-wrapped parts. Check each description against that.

column9: Because a prokaryotic cell has no nucleus, its DNA floats freely in the ___.
column20: cytoplasm|cytosol|the cytoplasm|nucleoid|nucleoid region|the nucleoid|the nucleoid region
column28: With no nucleus to hold it, prokaryotic DNA is free in the cytoplasm, the gel-like material inside the cell membrane. (Some books call the part of the cytoplasm where the loop sits the nucleoid region.) In eukaryotes the DNA is inside the nucleus.
column29: It is the gel-like material that fills the cell inside the cell membrane.

column9: Kayla studies an electron microscope image of a cell. It has a cell wall, ribosomes, and DNA, but no nucleus. What kind of cell is it most likely?
column14: A bacterium
column15: A plant cell
column16: An animal cell
column17: A fungus cell
column28: No nucleus means prokaryote, so the cell is a bacterium. Plant, animal, and fungus cells are all eukaryotic, so each of them would have a nucleus.
column29: Which single clue in the description decides prokaryote vs. eukaryote?

column9: A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria, and lysosomes, but no cell wall and no chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it?
column14: A bacterium
column15: A plant cell
column16: An animal cell
column17: A fungus cell
column28: A nucleus and membrane-bound organelles mean it is eukaryotic. With no cell wall and no chloroplasts, it is an animal cell. Plant and fungus cells would both have a cell wall, and a bacterium would have no nucleus.
column29: First decide prokaryote or eukaryote, then decide plant or animal.

column9: Which statement correctly compares the two cell types?
column14: Prokaryotes have a nucleus and organelles; eukaryotes do not.
column15: Eukaryotes have no ribosomes at all; only prokaryotes have them.
column16: Eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes do not.
column17: Prokaryotes are larger and more complex.
column28: Eukaryotes have a nucleus and many membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes have neither. Both have ribosomes, and prokaryotes are smaller and simpler.
column29: Check each choice against "pro means no."

column9: Which structures do prokaryotic AND eukaryotic cells both have? Select all that apply.
column14: Nucleus
column15: Ribosomes
column16: Cytoplasm
column17: Mitochondria
column28: All cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA. Only eukaryotes have a nucleus and mitochondria.
column29: For each structure, ask whether a bacterium has it too. Structures wrapped in their own membrane are found only in eukaryotes.

column9: A typical bacterium is about 2 µm long. A human egg cell is about 120 µm across. How many times larger is the egg cell than the bacterium?
column28: Divide the larger size by the smaller size: 120 µm ÷ 2 µm = 60. The egg cell is about 60 times larger. Eukaryotic cells are usually much larger than prokaryotic cells.
column29: "How many times larger" means divide the bigger number by the smaller number.

column9: Put these cells in order from smallest to largest. Watch the units: some sizes are in mm and some are in µm (1 mm = 1,000 µm).
column14: Human cheek cell (60 µm)
column15: Yeast cell (5 µm)
column16: Red blood cell (0.008 mm)
column17: Human egg cell (0.12 mm)
column28: Change every size to µm first: the red blood cell is 0.008 mm × 1,000 = 8 µm, and the egg cell is 0.12 mm × 1,000 = 120 µm. Then 2 < 5 < 8 < 60 < 120: bacterium, yeast cell, red blood cell, cheek cell, egg cell. The mm numbers only look small, because a millimeter is 1,000 times longer than a micrometer. The only prokaryote, the bacterium, is the smallest.
column29: Change every size to µm before you compare them.

column9: Why can eukaryotic cells carry out more complex jobs than prokaryotic cells?
column14: Their organelles let different jobs happen in separate compartments.
column15: They have no DNA, so they have much more room inside for organelles.
column16: They are smaller, so materials move through them faster.
column17: They lack ribosomes, so they do not waste energy making proteins.
column28: Membrane-bound organelles act like separate rooms, so jobs like releasing energy from food, packaging proteins, and breaking down waste can happen at the same time without getting in each other's way. Eukaryotes do have DNA and ribosomes, and they are larger, not smaller.
column29: What do eukaryotes have that prokaryotes lack, and how would that help a cell do many jobs at once?

column9: All single-celled organisms are prokaryotes.
column28: False. Being one cell does not make an organism a prokaryote. Amoebas and paramecia are each a single cell, but each one has a nucleus, so they are eukaryotes.
column29: Can you think of a single-celled organism that has a nucleus?

column9: Yeast is a fungus made of a single cell that has a nucleus. How should yeast be classified?
column14: A unicellular prokaryote
column15: A multicellular prokaryote
column16: A unicellular eukaryote
column17: A multicellular eukaryote
column28: It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote. It is one cell, so it is unicellular. A prokaryote would have no nucleus, and multicellular means many cells.
column29: Make two decisions: nucleus or no nucleus, and one cell or many.

column9: Which pair correctly lists a prokaryote first and a eukaryote second?
column14: Mushroom, then bacterium
column15: Bacterium, then mushroom
column16: Amoeba, then oak tree
column17: Human, then yeast
column28: A bacterium is a prokaryote and a mushroom (fungus) is a eukaryote. The reversed pair is backwards, and amoeba, oak tree, human, and yeast are all eukaryotes.
column29: Only one group of examples is prokaryotic. Find the pair that starts with it.

column9: Picture a prokaryote as a one-room studio apartment, where the kitchen, bed, and couch all share one open space, and a eukaryote as a house with many rooms. In this analogy, what part of a prokaryotic cell is the one open room?
column14: The nucleus, which holds all of the cell's DNA
column15: The cell wall, which surrounds the whole cell
column16: The cytoplasm, which fills the space inside the membrane
column17: The mitochondria, where the cell releases energy
column28: In the studio, everything shares one open space. In a prokaryote, the DNA and everything else inside the cell membrane share one space too: the cytoplasm. A prokaryote has no nucleus and no mitochondria, and a cell wall is a boundary around the outside, not a space inside.
column29: Cross off any choice a prokaryote does not have. Then ask: is the room a boundary, or the space inside it?

column9: Prokaryotes such as bacteria reproduce by copying their DNA and splitting into two cells. This is called binary ___.
column28: Binary fission means splitting in two. A bacterium copies its circular DNA and divides into two identical cells.
column29: Binary means two. The second word means splitting apart.

column9: Which structure can be found in some prokaryotes AND in some eukaryotes?
column14: A nucleus
column15: A cell wall
column16: Mitochondria
column17: A Golgi apparatus
column28: Bacteria have cell walls, and so do plants and fungi (eukaryotes). A nucleus, mitochondria, and a Golgi apparatus are found only in eukaryotes.
column29: For each choice ask two questions: could a bacterium have it, and could any eukaryote have it?

column9: A scientist finds a new cell that is only 1 µm long. Before looking any closer, what is the best prediction?
column14: Probably a eukaryote, since eukaryotes are usually much smaller.
column15: Probably a prokaryote, since prokaryotes are usually much smaller.
column16: Probably a plant cell, since a stiff cell wall keeps plant cells small.
column17: Probably an animal cell, since animal cells have no wall and can be tiny.
column28: Bacteria are only a few µm long, while most eukaryotic cells are 10 to 100 µm or more. A 1 µm cell is most likely a prokaryote, though you would still need to check for a nucleus. Eukaryotes are usually larger, not smaller, and plant and animal cells are eukaryotic, so they are usually far bigger than 1 µm.
column29: Compare 1 µm to the sizes you know: bacterium about 2 µm, cheek cell about 60 µm.

column9: Match each organism to its description.
column14: E. coli :: Prokaryote, always one cell
column15: Yeast :: Eukaryote made of one cell
column16: Oak tree :: Multicellular eukaryote with cell walls and chloroplasts
column17: Human :: Multicellular eukaryote with no cell walls
column28: E. coli is a bacterium (prokaryote, one cell). Yeast is a single-celled fungus (eukaryote). An oak tree is a plant (cell walls and chloroplasts). A human is an animal (no cell walls).
column29: Decide prokaryote or eukaryote first, then one cell or many, then plant or animal.

column9: A student says, "Strep throat bacteria need energy, so their cells must have mitochondria." What is wrong with this idea?
column14: Bacteria do not need any energy, so they have no way to make it.
column15: Bacteria get all of their energy from reactions inside their nucleus.
column16: Bacteria have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria to make their energy.
column17: Bacteria have no mitochondria; they release energy in their cytoplasm.
column28: All living cells need energy, but prokaryotes have no mitochondria. The energy reactions happen in their cytoplasm and on their cell membrane. Bacteria have no nucleus, and they have no chloroplasts either.
column29: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles. Do prokaryotes have any of those?

column9: The first living things on Earth were most likely prokaryotes.
column28: True. Prokaryotes are the simplest cells, and the oldest fossils of cells look like bacteria. More complex eukaryotic cells came later.
column29: Which type of cell is simpler? Simple things usually come first.

column9: A biologist describes four organisms. **P:** one cell, no nucleus, has a cell wall. **Q:** one cell with a nucleus, lives in pond water. **R:** many cells, each with a nucleus and a cell wall. **S:** one cell, no nucleus, lives in a hot spring. Which list contains ONLY eukaryotes?
column14: P and R
column15: Q and S
column16: P and S
column17: Q and R
column28: The nucleus decides. Q and R each have a nucleus, so both are eukaryotes; Q is only one cell, but some eukaryotes are unicellular. P and S have no nucleus, so they are prokaryotes, and P's cell wall doesn't make it a plant.
column29: Sort each organism by one clue only: nucleus or no nucleus. Don't let the other details distract you.

column9: Researchers pull the DNA out of two unknown cells. Sample 1 is a single closed loop. Sample 2 is twelve separate straight (linear) pieces. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Sample 2's cell kept its DNA inside a nucleus.
column15: Sample 1's cell kept its DNA inside a nucleus.
column16: Sample 2's cell came from a multicellular organism.
column17: Both cells kept their DNA free in the cytoplasm.
column28: Linear chromosomes are the eukaryote pattern, and eukaryotes keep their chromosomes inside a nucleus, so Sample 2's cell had a nucleus. A single loop is the prokaryote pattern, so Sample 1's DNA sat free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus. The number of DNA pieces doesn't tell you how many cells the organism has, since single-celled eukaryotes have several chromosomes too.
column29: Match each DNA shape to a cell type first. Then ask where that cell type keeps its DNA.

column9: A chemical passes easily through cell walls and cell membranes. Once inside a cell, it destroys only the membrane around the nucleus. Which of these cells would it leave undamaged?
column14: Amoeba cells, since one-celled organisms keep their DNA loose
column15: Mushroom cells, since fungi keep their DNA in a single loop
column16: Human skin cells, since animal cells have no cell wall at all
column17: Yogurt bacteria, since bacteria have no nucleus at all
column28: The chemical can only damage a nucleus, and bacteria have none, so there is nothing for it to destroy. Amoebas are single cells but still have a nucleus, and fungi keep linear chromosomes inside a nucleus. Skin cells have a nucleus too, and a missing cell wall doesn't protect them, because the chemical passes through walls anyway.
column29: Ask of each cell: does it have a nucleus? Don't let the reasons written in the choices distract you.

column9: An antibiotic kills bacteria by blocking their ribosomes, but it does not harm the patient's own cells, which also have ribosomes. What is the best explanation?
column14: Human cells do not have any ribosomes, so nothing is blocked.
column15: Human ribosomes are inside the nucleus, where the drug can't reach.
column16: The antibiotic only works on cells that have a cell wall.
column17: Bacterial ribosomes are smaller and shaped differently.
column28: Both cell types have ribosomes, but prokaryotic ribosomes are smaller and built differently, so a drug can fit bacterial ribosomes without fitting human ones. Human cells do have ribosomes, and they are found in the cytoplasm and on the rough ER, not hidden in the nucleus. This drug targets ribosomes, not walls.
column29: Both cells have ribosomes. For the drug to pick only one, what must be different?

column9: Penicillin kills bacteria by attacking their cell walls. Why doesn't penicillin damage human cells?
column14: Human cells have no cell wall for penicillin to attack.
column15: Human cells have a thicker cell wall than bacteria.
column16: Human cells have no cell membrane for it to attack.
column17: Human cells are prokaryotic, so penicillin can't reach them.
column28: Animal cells, including human cells, have only a cell membrane and no cell wall, so a drug that attacks cell walls has nothing to attack. Human cells do have a membrane, and they are eukaryotic.
column29: Which of these structures do animal cells have: cell membrane, cell wall, or both?

column9: A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria, and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. It came from an organism that cannot make its own food. What kind of organism did it come from?
column14: A fungus, such as a mushroom
column15: A bacterium, such as E. coli
column16: An animal, such as a frog
column17: A plant, such as a maple tree
column28: The nucleus and mitochondria mean the cell is eukaryotic, which rules out a bacterium. The cell wall rules out an animal. A maple tree makes its own food by photosynthesis, so the food clue rules out the plant. That leaves a fungus: fungus cells have a nucleus and a cell wall but no chloroplasts, and fungi take in food from what they grow on.
column29: Use each clue to cross off one choice: the nucleus, the cell wall, and how the organism gets its food.

column9: A student says, "Prokaryotes are less successful than eukaryotes because they don't have a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles." What is the best response?
column14: The student is right; prokaryotes can't survive without a nucleus.
column15: The student is wrong, because prokaryotes are more complex than eukaryotes.
column16: The student is right; prokaryotes can't carry out life processes on their own.
column17: The student is wrong; prokaryotes are simpler but thrive almost everywhere.
column28: Simple is not the same as unsuccessful. Bacteria thrive in soil, water, hot springs, and inside your body, and they were among the first life on Earth. Each one carries out every life process on its own without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; its ribosomes and chemical reactions share the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes are simpler than eukaryotes, not more complex.
column29: Being simpler and being successful are two different things.

column9: Two unknown cells were examined. Data table: Cell X: nucleus = no, ribosomes = yes, mitochondria = no, size = 30 µm | Cell Y: nucleus = yes, ribosomes = yes, mitochondria = yes, size = 1 µm. How should the cells be classified?
column14: X is eukaryotic and Y is prokaryotic.
column15: X is prokaryotic and Y is eukaryotic.
column16: Both cells are prokaryotic.
column17: Both cells are eukaryotic.
column28: The nucleus decides, not the size. Cell X has no nucleus, so it is prokaryotic even though it is unusually large; a few kinds of bacteria grow this big. Cell Y has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic even though it is tiny; some ocean algae cells are only about 1 µm across. Size is only a first guess, and ribosomes don't help decide, because every cell has them.
column29: Which clue in the table decides the cell type for certain? Don't let the other columns pull you away from it.

column9: Which observations would prove that a cell is eukaryotic? Select all that apply.
column14: It has a chloroplast
column15: It has ribosomes
column16: It has DNA
column17: It has a lysosome
column28: Chloroplasts, lysosomes, and endoplasmic reticulum are membrane-bound organelles, which only eukaryotes have, so seeing any one of them proves the cell is eukaryotic. Ribosomes and DNA are in every cell, and bacteria have cell walls just like plants and fungi, so those can't tell the two types apart.
column29: Cross off anything a bacterium could also have. Whatever is left is wrapped in its own membrane.

column9: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes that carry out photosynthesis, but they have no chloroplasts. What does this show?
column14: Cyanobacteria should be classified as plants, since they make their own food.
column15: Cyanobacteria must carry out photosynthesis inside their mitochondria.
column16: Some prokaryotes can do complex jobs without membrane-bound organelles.
column17: Photosynthesis must be a simple job, since a prokaryote is able to do it.
column28: Cyanobacteria have no nucleus and no chloroplasts, yet they make sugar from sunlight using pigments on folded membranes inside the cell. So complex jobs don't always need membrane-bound organelles. They are prokaryotes, not plants (plant cells are eukaryotic), they have no mitochondria, and photosynthesis is a complex, many-step job no matter which cell does it.
column29: Plant cells need chloroplasts for this many-step job, yet cyanobacteria do it with none. Which choice fits that fact and still treats them as prokaryotes?

column9: In a cell-factory analogy, the nucleus is the manager's office that holds the blueprints (DNA), and ribosomes are the workers who build the products (proteins). True or false: In this analogy, a prokaryotic cell would be a workshop with no manager's office, where the blueprints lie out on the open floor and there are no workers at all.
column28: False. Part of the picture is right: a prokaryote has no nucleus, so its DNA (the blueprints) lies free in the cytoplasm, like blueprints out on the open floor. The "no workers" part is wrong. Every cell has ribosomes, because every cell has to make proteins, so a prokaryote's workers are right there on the floor with its blueprints. A workshop with no workers could never build anything.
column29: Check each part of the picture on its own: the manager's office, the blueprints, and the workers. Does a prokaryote have each one?

column9: Sofia looks at her cheek cells and some bacteria at 400×. She can clearly see the nucleus in each cheek cell, but the bacteria look like tiny dots. What is the best explanation?
column14: Bacteria are much smaller than cheek cells and have no nucleus to see.
column15: The bacteria are dead, so they look like dots.
column16: Bacteria are larger than cheek cells, so they are blurry and out of focus.
column17: Cheek cells are prokaryotic, so they are easier to see.
column28: A bacterium is about 2 µm and a cheek cell about 60 µm, around 30 times bigger. At 400× the bacteria are still tiny, and they have no nucleus to show. Cheek cells are eukaryotic.
column29: Compare the sizes: a bacterium is about 2 µm and a cheek cell is about 60 µm.

column9: Euglena lives in ponds as a single cell. It has a nucleus, mitochondria, and chloroplasts, and it swims with a whiplike flagellum. It has no cell wall. Which classification fits ALL of these clues?
column14: A prokaryote, since it is one cell that swims with a flagellum
column15: A plant cell, since it has chloroplasts and makes its own food
column16: An animal cell, since it has no cell wall and swims on its own
column17: A single-celled eukaryote that is neither a plant nor an animal
column28: The nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, chloroplasts) make Euglena a eukaryote, and it is one cell, so it is unicellular. It can't be a plant cell, because plant cells have a cell wall, and it can't be an animal cell, because animal cells have no chloroplasts. That is why Euglena is classified as a protist. Being single-celled or having a flagellum doesn't make something a prokaryote.
column29: Test each choice against every clue, not just one. Which choice clashes with none of them?

column9: Marcus builds a model of a bacterium. It has a cell wall, a cell membrane, ribosomes, and a round nucleus in the middle with the DNA inside. What should he change?
column14: Remove the ribosomes, because bacteria do not make proteins.
column15: Remove the cell wall, because only plants have walls.
column16: Remove the nucleus and show the DNA as a loop free in the cytoplasm.
column17: Add mitochondria, because every living cell needs them to make energy.
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes, so the nucleus has to go; the DNA should be a circular loop in the cytoplasm. Bacteria do have ribosomes and cell walls, and they have no mitochondria.
column29: Go through his model part by part and ask: would a real bacterium have this?

column9: A typical bacterium is about 2 µm long. A grain of sand is 0.5 mm across. How many bacteria could line up end to end across the grain of sand? (1 mm = 1,000 µm)
column28: First change units: 0.5 mm × 1,000 = 500 µm. Then divide by the length of one bacterium: 500 µm ÷ 2 µm = 250 bacteria. That is why you need a microscope to see them.
column29: Change 0.5 mm to µm first, then divide by the length of one bacterium.

column9: Data table: bacterium 2 µm (prokaryote), yeast 5 µm, red blood cell 8 µm, cheek cell 60 µm, egg cell 120 µm (all eukaryotes). Mason concludes, "This proves every prokaryote is smaller than every eukaryote." What is the best evaluation?
column14: He is right, because the bacterium is the smallest of the five cells in the table.
column15: He is wrong to say "proves," because the table measures only one prokaryote.
column16: He is right, because five cells are enough data to prove a pattern.
column17: He is wrong, because the yeast cell is smaller than the red blood cell.
column28: The table fits his idea, but it measures only one prokaryote, and one example can't prove a rule about every cell. The yeast cell being smaller than the red blood cell is true but beside the point, since both are eukaryotes. In fact his claim is false: some giant bacteria, such as Thiomargarita, can be seen without a microscope and are larger than most eukaryotic cells.
column29: How many prokaryotes did the table actually measure?

column9: Trees, mushrooms, and humans are large organisms made of many specialized cells. Why are all such large organisms eukaryotes?
column14: Eukaryotic cells are smaller, so more of them can pack into one body.
column15: Eukaryotic organelles let cells become larger, more complex, and specialized.
column16: Prokaryotic cells can't release energy, so they can't power a big body.
column17: Prokaryotic cells have no cell membrane, so they can't stick together.
column28: Building muscles, leaves, or roots takes cells that can grow larger and take on special jobs, and the membrane-bound organelles of eukaryotic cells make that possible. Prokaryotes are always single cells. They do release energy and do have a cell membrane, and eukaryotic cells are larger than prokaryotic cells, not smaller.
column29: Prokaryotes are always one cell. What do eukaryotic cells have that lets them divide up jobs?

column9: Scientists find a single-celled organism living in an animal's gut. Its DNA is inside a nucleus, but the cell has no mitochondria. Dev says, "No mitochondria, so it must be a prokaryote." Nia says, "It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote." Which evaluation is best?
column14: Dev is right, because only eukaryotic cells have mitochondria.
column15: Nia is right, because a cell living in an animal is an animal cell.
column16: Nia is right, because having a nucleus is what makes a cell eukaryotic.
column17: Dev is right, because an organism made of one cell is a prokaryote.
column28: Nia is right. A cell with its DNA inside a nucleus is eukaryotic, even if it is missing other organelles. Dev's logic runs backwards: only eukaryotes have mitochondria, but that doesn't mean every eukaryote has them. Scientists really have found a gut microbe like this one (Monocercomonoides), a eukaryote with no mitochondria at all. Being one cell doesn't make something a prokaryote, and living inside an animal doesn't make a cell an animal cell.
column29: Only eukaryotes have mitochondria, but does every eukaryote have to? Find the clue that settles the cell type for certain.
